subject: gorilla
title: 83% of Radiologists Missed a Gorilla Hidden in a Lung Scan

scenes.text: Doctors stared straight at a gorilla and didn't see it.
Researchers gave 24 radiologists real lung scans and asked them to hunt for cancer nodules.
In one scan they had hidden a picture of a gorilla, 48 times bigger than a typical nodule.
Twenty of the 24 never noticed it. That's 83 percent.
Eye tracking showed most of them had looked right at it.
It's called inattentional blindness. Your brain shows you what you're hunting for, and quietly drops the rest.

description:
Trained radiologists looked straight at a gorilla and did not see it.
In a 2013 study, psychologist Trafton Drew and colleagues asked 24 experienced radiologists to search CT scans of lungs for cancer nodules. Into one scan they had inserted an image of a gorilla about the size of a matchbook, 48 times larger than a typical nodule. Twenty of the 24 (83 percent) did not report it, even though eye tracking showed most of them had looked directly at it. The effect is called inattentional blindness, made famous by the original invisible gorilla video, in which about half of viewers counting basketball passes miss a person in a gorilla suit walking through the game.
Would you have spotted it? Comment below.
first_comment: When the radiologists were shown the scan again afterwards, every one of them saw the gorilla. Would you have spotted it?
